This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lyndi Kenyon. Big Tech Company Invidia says its CEO
Jensen Wong is stepping down. The company's current executive vice president and chief
financial officer will serve as interim CEO. NPR's John Ruich reports.
The decision follows a flurry of reports from the New York Times and others alleging that
Wong had had an extramarital affair with an executive at Invidia and a separate one with
a client who U.S. intelligence officials believed was recruited by China's government to spy on him.
NPR has not independently confirmed those reports. The departure ends a long career for Wong, who
co-founded Invidia 33 years ago and oversaw its rise to become one of the world's biggest and
most important companies. News of Wong's affairs has rattled markets and Invidia's share price has
taken a beating in recent days. John Ruich, NPR News. Democrat Scott Colom will be the next U.S.
senator from Mississippi. NPR's Stephen Fowler takes a look at Colom's victory.
Black turnout surged in the South this year, but it really surged in Mississippi,
the state with the highest share of black voters in the country.
Several majority black counties in Mississippi saw a higher Democratic turnout this year than
the presidential race in 2024. And overall, Colom earned about 6,600 more raw votes this year than
former Vice President Kamala Harris. That's more than his margin over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
On the other side of the equation, Republican turnout plummeted with Hyde-Smith receiving closer
to 300,000 votes fewer than President Trump, thanks to a combination of people switching
their support to Colom and Republicans just staying home. Stephen Fowler, NPR News.
Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky says there are speed restrictions once again affecting
star shield. That's the military version of the Starlink satellite service the Ukrainian
military uses on the front lines. NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports. Zelensky warned the restrictions
are helping Russia carry out more accurate attacks and causing further Ukrainian casualties.
He also said the restrictions have affected Ukrainian military operations for several days
across the entire front line and that the speed restrictions that kick in at 100 miles an hour
make it more difficult to intercept Russia's new jet-powered drones. Zelensky said the speed
restrictions are not due to random technical errors, but are systematic. They come just as
the U.S. is again pushing negotiations to try to end the war. Star Shield was first restricted
three weeks ago as President Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia, then it was reinstated.
It has never been clear whether Trump or Starlink owner Elon Musk slowed the system down.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kyiv. Negotiators Janet Kushner and Steve
Whitcoff are in Moscow meeting with Russia's President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin.
On Wall Street at last check, the Dow is up nearly 166 points. The Nasdaq is up 31.
You're listening to NPR.
The American Cancer Society is changing its prostate screening guidelines
and is now recommending regular PSA blood test screenings. NPR's Yuki Neguchi reports.
The Cancer Society previously recommended patients talk to their doctors and share decision-making
about whether to screen for prostate cancer, which will be diagnosed in roughly 333,000
Americans this year. Now, based on new data, it recommends PSA tests every other year for
men between 50 and 69. And annual screenings, starting at age 45, for those at high risk,
like black men and people with strong family history. One concern was that prostate cancer,
which can be harmless in many men, was being overtreated, causing more harm than good.
To prevent that, the Cancer Society is also recommending MRI and additional blood tests
before getting a biopsy. Yuki Neguchi, NPR News.
Lawmakers in Spain have ratified new housing measures aimed at limiting evictions and real
estate speculation. These measures come just one day after a general strike and major protests
over the high cost of housing in Spain. Since the rules were passed by Spain's interim lower
house of parliament, they could be revised depending upon the outcome of this month's
general election. The conservative popular party has vowed to repeal those housing changes
if it is the party that wins election in those upcoming elections.
Now, this election is set for November 29th. I'm Lyndy Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
